tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file outside the working directory that you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your turn is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

"""Mechanical pre-promotion lint for Flint staged library folders.

Usage: python scripts/lint_library.py <book-folder> [<book-folder> ...]
Checks: body em dashes (header separators allowed), unresolved [[links]] (against staging
library + vault), review-history narration, confidence values, required sections.
"""
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

STAGING = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "staging" / "library"
VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")
HEADER = re.compile(r"^\*\*[^*]+\*\* —")
HISTORY = re.compile(r"prior version|earlier draft|NO-GO|round[- ]1|round[- ]2|fix pass|fixer|this revision|previous version", re.I)
CONF = {"proven", "supported", "untested", "contested"}
SECTIONS = ["**What it is**", "**When NOT to apply**"]

known = set()
for root in (STAGING, VAULT):
    for p in root.rglob("*.md"):
        known.add(p.stem)
        known.add(p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix())
        known.add(p.parent.name + "/" + p.stem)

problems = 0
for folder in sys.argv[1:]:
    for f in sorted(Path(folder).glob("*.md")):
        text = f.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        issues = []
        body_dash = [i + 1 for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines())
                     if "—" in HEADER.sub("", line)]
        if body_dash:
            issues.append(f"body em dash lines {body_dash[:8]}")
        for link in re.findall(r"\[\[([^\]|#]+)", text):
            link = link.strip().removesuffix(".md")
            if link not in known and link.split("/")[-1] not in known:
                issues.append(f"unresolved [[{link}]]")
        if not f.name.startswith("_"):
            m = re.search(r"^confidence:\s*(\S+)", text, re.M)
            if not m or m.group(1).strip("\"'") not in CONF:
                issues.append(f"confidence={m.group(1) if m else 'missing'}")
            for s in SECTIONS:
                if s not in text:
                    issues.append(f"missing {s}")
            h = HISTORY.findall(text)
            if h:
                issues.append(f"review-history words {sorted(set(x.lower() for x in h))}")
        if issues:
            problems += len(issues)
            print(f"{f.parent.name}/{f.name}: " + "; ".join(issues))
print(f"TOTAL ISSUES: {problems}")

# Verkhoshansky's Activation Levels: Training, Quiet, High, Over-Activation, Stress, and the Threshold of Adaptability

**What it is** — Following the homeostasis/allostasis material earlier in the same lecture
(see [[framework--homeostasis-vs-allostasis-mcewen-sterling]]), Evans's slides (U1 L4
p.26-32), all credited "Verkhoshansky, 2012," present a training-load-response model. A
supercompensation diagram (p.26) shows repeated "Training work-out" -> "Body's hyperfunction"
-> "Repetitive work-recovery phases" (proteins depletion during work, re-synthesis during
recovery, each cycle net-positive) -> "Performance increasing," paired with a "Main aims of
training load flows" box mapping Strength, Speed, Aerobic Endurance, and Speed Endurance to
specific protein-synthesis targets (contractile protein; sarcoplasmic reticulum protein;
mitochondrial protein; proteins with buffer capacity and isoferment resistance to pH
decrease), then "Specific proteins depletion" -> "Increasing the specific proteins contents in
working organs thanks to the phenomenon of Supercompensation" -> "Specific
morphological-functional restructuring the athlete's body." A second chart (p.27) plots
Workability state, Metabolic processes activity, and Catabolic processes activity all rising
with training load, against a dotted Anabolic processes curve that rises then falls, overlaid
on five load bands: Training, Quiet Activation, High Activation, Over-Activation, Stress. A
third chart (p.28) adds "Critical level of homeostasis disturbance" and "Threshold of
adaptability" markers at the Over-Activation/Stress boundary, with the text: "When the
training load impact provokes the Over-Activation reaction, the prevalence of anabolic process
switches to catabolic. This change indicates the Threshold of adaptability has been surpassed,
which is also related to critical level of Homeostasis disturbance." Two further slides
("Ability for Athlete to Adapt," p.29-30) recast this as a balance-scale diagram (Constant
homeostasis disturbance versus Constant homeostasis re-establishing = Allostasis; the
imbalance = Allostatic load), with text: "Similarly, during execution of a training exercise,
surpassing the anaerobic threshold brings about glycolysis and the subsequent decrease in the
body's workability. During the training process, reaching beyond a certain level of training
load initiates stress syndrome and a consequent decrease in the body's adaptability" (p.29,
restated with near-identical wording on p.30, which also maps Low/Medium/High/Excessive load
onto Training/Activation/Stress states and Quiet/High/Over-Activation). Two final slides
(p.31-32) show "Subsequent loads impacts," each an arrow diagram of repeated training loads
against a "Critical level of homeostasis disturbance" line, with "Allostatic overload" marked
once the accumulated load supersedes that line: "Accumulation of allostatic load, which
supersedes the critical level of homeostatic disturbance, results in activation of the
emergency systems: allostatic overload" (p.31); "The human body cannot maintain such
allostatic load for very long without consequences. In the long run, allostatic changes may
fail to be adaptive as the maintenance of allostasis changes over a long period" (p.32). No
book title is given beyond "Verkhoshansky" and the year 2012.

shift from anabolic-dominant to catabolic-dominant processes (the "threshold of adaptability")
and that sustained allostatic load past that point produces "allostatic overload," but they do
not give a specific physiological mechanism for why this particular crossover happens where it
does, or how to measure "Over-Activation" versus "Stress" for a real athlete; the curves and

resets its operating level rather than simply recovering to the old one), but Evans does not
state this synthesis explicitly; it is the entry writer's reading across p.17-32 of this
lecture.

load-response spectrum: is a given session or block within the Training/Quiet/High-Activation

bands, a named crossover point) that the baseline material does not spell out.

# Buzzichelli's Load Progression (Wave Loading) and Specificity Continuum (Complex Versus Sequential Training Means)

**What it is** — Continuing the same "Periodization of Conditional Motor Capacities"
framework cited to "Buzzichelli, 2011" (U3 L5 p.26, see also
[[framework--buzzichelli-integration-and-development-of-motor-capacities]]), two further
components are given, each an image slide with a bar chart. Load Progression, "WAVE LOADING"
(p.31), titled "Load within the mesocycle / Load within the microcycle": a four-panel bar
chart (Micro 1-4 on a 0-6 scale, read from the chart) for four loading patterns - Ascending
Ond.: Micro1 4, Micro2 3, Micro3 5, Micro4 2.5; Descending Ond.: Micro1 5, Micro2 3, Micro3 4,
Micro4 2.5; Step Loading: Micro1 3, Micro2 4, Micro3 5, Micro4 2.5; Flat Loading: Micro1-3
roughly 4.5 each, Micro4 2.5. Load Progression in a Competitive Microcycle (Weekly Match)
(p.32): a seven-day bar chart (0-120 scale, read from the chart) - Mon 50, Tue 85, Wed 100,
Thu 85, Fri 55, Sat 55, Sun 100. Specificity of the Training Means (p.33): a two-way
distinction between "Complex" ("General And Specific Training Means Are Utilized At The Same
Time") and "Sequential" ("General Training Means Precede Specific Training Means"), each
illustrated with its own annual-plan-style bar/line chart but no further numeric labels. No
book title is given beyond "Buzzichelli, 2011."

**Why it works** — The p.31 chart names "wave loading" and gives four patterns (Ascending
Ond., Descending Ond., Step Loading, Flat Loading) at two timescales without stating a
mechanism for why a wave pattern (as opposed to, for example, a linear pattern; see the
vault's Bompa `framework--step-loading-paradigm.md` for a different named loading scheme) is
preferred at either the mesocycle or microcycle level. The Specificity distinction states
that general training means can either precede specific ones (Sequential) or run
concurrently (Complex), which mirrors the same general-to-specific structure found in
Bondarchuk's GPE/SPE/SDE/CE exercise-class continuum (already staged in this library at
`transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes.md`),
though Evans's slide does not explicitly connect the two. Step and flat loading appear as
panels on the same slide captioned "Wave Loading" (p.31); the slide does not say whether step
loading is a kind of wave loading or a separately-named scheme placed on the same chart.

**When to apply** — As a two-question check when programming a training block: is the load
progression across the mesocycle or microcycle following a deliberate wave pattern (rather
than, implicitly, a flat or purely linear one), and are general and specific training means
being run concurrently or in sequence? Eric's baseline: its own preferred model is
"undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week
(e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks)," stated as "a more preferential model
to use" in the course transcript material (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26`, itself Inferred/unconfirmed as Eric's
individual position per that baseline's tension log). Inference: this is a specific, named
example of exactly the "wave loading" concept this Evans slide names and, unlike the entry
writer's earlier reading, does supply numbers of its own (the p.31 Ascending/Descending
Ond./Step/Flat bar values above); Eric's baseline's four-week undulating example remains the
closest specific numeric illustration outside this course, though it comes from a different,
Inferred-provenance source.

**When NOT to apply** — The p.31 and p.32 values above were read from bar charts,
not printed as text on the slide, so treat them as approximate. No page number is given for
"Buzzichelli, 2011," so this cannot be verified against a primary source. Confidence is
untested.

**Example** — The p.31 wave-loading bars (Ascending Ond., Descending Ond., Step Loading, Flat
Loading, values above) and the p.32 competitive-microcycle bars (Mon-Sun, values above) are
the lecture's worked numeric examples.

**Related** — [[framework--buzzichelli-integration-and-development-of-motor-capacities]].
Reciprocal-link suggestion:
`periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm.md` (a different named loading scheme
from the same domain, worth comparing against "wave loading" now that both are numerically
detailed) and
`transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes.md`
(the general-to-specific exercise continuum this Specificity component structurally parallels).
</content>

14	# Worked Example: A Wide Receiver's Preparatory-Phase Weekly Loading Template
15	
16	**What it is** — Continuing the hypothetical "American Football, Wide Receiver" annual-plan
17	example from U3 L7 (see
18	[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]), Evans's slide (U3 L8 p.2) first
19	gives the phase's content plan by sub-phase: Exercises (GPE & SPE - General; GPE & SPE & SDE -
20	Specific); Energetics (Alactic Power & Aerobic Capacity - General; Alactic Capacity*, Alactic
21	Power* & Aerobic Capacity - Specific); Biomotor, General sub-phase (Primary: Flexibility/
22	Mobility & Muscular Endurance; Secondary: Speed [acceleration qualities], Maximal Strength
23	[accumulation weights]; Tertiary: Skill) and Specific sub-phase (Primary: Maximal Strength
24	[lineman, possibly Wide Receiver], Speed [acceleration, longer distances for WR]; Secondary:
25	Muscular endurance [via weights, running drills, etc], Skill; Tertiary: Flexibility/
26	Mobility). He then gives a specific weekly structure for two preparatory sub-phases.
27	Preparatory I, General (p.3-4, 11-12): duration 4-5 weeks, training days Monday/Tuesday/
28	Thursday/Friday, 8 hours per week ("CARA" - Countable Athletically Related Activities), indoor
29	turf and weight room available at all times; loading by day - Sunday/Wednesday/Saturday off
30	(Small), Monday Medium, Tuesday Substantial-Large, Thursday Medium, Friday Substantial-Large;
31	session focus - Monday/Thursday "Aerobic Capacity / UB Focus" (extensive runs, upper body
32	weights, extensive medicine-ball throws, torso work), Tuesday/Friday "Alactic Power / LB
33	Focus" (sprints, jumps, intensive medicine-ball throws, lower body weights). Preparatory I,
34	Specific (p.13-16): duration 3-4 weeks, same weekly structure and facilities, loading by day -
35	Sunday/Wednesday/Saturday off (Small), Monday Medium, Tuesday "Substantial-Large/Extreme,"
36	Thursday Medium, Friday Substantial-Large; session focus unchanged (Monday/Thursday Aerobic
37	Capacity/UB with "Extensive Runs/Drills" replacing plain "Extensive Runs," Tuesday/Friday
38	Alactic Power/LB with "Sprints/Drills" replacing plain "Sprints").
39	
40	The reference material behind this template sits on five image slides (p.5-10). p.5, "High
41	Intensity Training Components" (velocity-by-distance curve plus a table of exercise types by
42	distance band: Strength, Power, Power-Speed, Speed [Elastic Power], Special Endurance). p.6,
43	"High Intensity Training For Sports," reprints the same distance chart with sport-by-sport
44	high-intensity distance bars read off the chart: 200m Sprinter to about 200m, 100m Sprinter to
45	about 100m, Soccer Player to about 90m, Hockey Player to about 60m, "Football Player - Back"
46	to about 65m, Basketball Player to about 50m, "Football Player - Line" to about 35m, Thrower
47	to about 25m, Olympic Lifter to about 15m (note the chart says "Back," not "wide receiver," so
48	this is a position-group figure, not WR-specific). p.7, "Motor Unit Involvement," a bar chart
49	of approximate percentage of an athlete's total motor units by exercise, from 100% (Clean &
50	Jerk / Maximal Sprints) down to 5% (Seated Row / Isolated Supplementary Lifts). p.8,
51	"Training Zones of Physical Capacity," a five-zone table (purpose, magnitude, training method,
52	energetics, HR, lactate) credited "Borilkievich, V. Physical capacity in extreme muscle
53	conditions. Leningrad, USSR, 1982." p.9, a Jovanovic/Prilepin effort-level and reps/sets/volume
54	chart credited "Copyright 2013 by Mladen Jovanovic." p.10, an energy-system work:rest table
55	(type, intensity, duration, rest interval, number of sets, across alactic and glycolytic power
56	and capacity and aerobic power and capacity) with no sport or author label on the slide.
57	
58	**Why it works** — Evans does not explain why this specific day-of-week loading pattern
59	(Tuesday and Friday as the two highest-load days, bracketing a Medium Monday and Thursday,
60	with three low/off days) was chosen over an alternative arrangement, nor why the General
61	sub-phase's 4-5 weeks shortens to 3-4 weeks in the Specific sub-phase; Inference: the
62	alactic-power/lower-body Tuesday-Friday pairing and aerobic-capacity/upper-body
63	Monday-Thursday pairing appears designed to separate the two energy-system emphases named in
64	the Step Five bioenergetic sequence (alactic and aerobic, see
65	[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]) onto different training days
66	rather than combining them in the same session, consistent with the general
67	training-compatibility logic in [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]], but this
68	specific rationale is not stated by Evans in this lecture.
69	
70	**When to apply** — As a concrete template for how a general-to-specific preparatory
71	progression can be laid out week-to-week for a skill-position football athlete, separating
72	aerobic-capacity/upper-body work from alactic-power/lower-body work by day. Eric's baseline
73	does not include a comparably detailed weekly loading template for any specific position.
74	`_book.md` records this course's Exam 3 Study Guide as cited once, for this entry, items 62
75	and 64-65 (see `_book.md` for the reconciliation); item 62 ("Alactic power speed distance
76	comparison between offensive lineman vs wide receiver") and items 64-65 (SPE/SDE lower-body
77	exercise choices for a wide receiver) confirm Evans intended a lineman-versus-wide-receiver
78	comparison as a further teaching point, but the specific comparative numbers for that
79	lineman/WR pairing were not found on the slide pages read for this ingest; the closest
80	figures actually on the slides are the p.6 "Back" versus "Line" position-group bars above, not
81	a lineman-versus-WR pairing.
82	
83	**When NOT to apply** — This is an illustrative teaching template for a
84	hypothetical wide receiver, not data from any real athlete, team, or season; no actual
85	performance outcomes, injury data, or adherence data are given anywhere in this lecture to
86	support that this specific loading pattern is effective. The "8 hours per week (CARA)" and
87	NCAA-specific facility-availability framing tie this template to US college athletics
88	countable-hours rules, which Evans references elsewhere in the course as a real constraint
89	("NCAA reality? CARA hours..." U3 L3 p.12, p.16) but does not re-explain in this lecture; a
90	reader unfamiliar with NCAA countable-athletically-related-activity rules should not assume
91	this 8-hour figure applies outside that specific regulatory context. "CARA" itself is not
92	expanded on this slide; Inference (NCAA term): Countable Athletically Related Activities is
93	the entry writer's outside expansion of the acronym, not stated by Evans on this slide.
94	Confidence is untested.
95	
96	**Example** — The weekly template itself, described above, plus the p.5-10 reference slides
97	(distance-by-intensity curve and sport bars, motor-unit-involvement chart, Borilkievich zones,
98	Jovanovic/Prilepin chart, energy-system work:rest table), is the example.
99

101	[[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]].
102	</content>

[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]), Evans's slide (U3 L8 p.2) first
gives the phase's content plan by sub-phase: Exercises (GPE & SPE - General; GPE & SPE & SDE -
Specific); Energetics (Alactic Power & Aerobic Capacity - General; Alactic Capacity*, Alactic
Power* & Aerobic Capacity - Specific); Biomotor, General sub-phase (Primary: Flexibility/
Mobility & Muscular Endurance; Secondary: Speed [acceleration qualities], Maximal Strength
[accumulation weights]; Tertiary: Skill) and Specific sub-phase (Primary: Maximal Strength
[lineman, possibly Wide Receiver], Speed [acceleration, longer distances for WR]; Secondary:
Muscular endurance [via weights, running drills, etc], Skill; Tertiary: Flexibility/
Mobility). He then gives a specific weekly structure for two preparatory sub-phases.
Preparatory I, General (p.3-4, 11-12): duration 4-5 weeks, training days Monday/Tuesday/
Thursday/Friday, 8 hours per week ("CARA" - Countable Athletically Related Activities), indoor
turf and weight room available at all times; loading by day - Sunday/Wednesday/Saturday off
(Small), Monday Medium, Tuesday Substantial-Large, Thursday Medium, Friday Substantial-Large;
session focus - Monday/Thursday "Aerobic Capacity / UB Focus" (extensive runs, upper body
weights, extensive medicine-ball throws, torso work), Tuesday/Friday "Alactic Power / LB
Focus" (sprints, jumps, intensive medicine-ball throws, lower body weights). Preparatory I,
Specific (p.13-16): duration 3-4 weeks, same weekly structure and facilities, loading by day -
Sunday/Wednesday/Saturday off (Small), Monday Medium, Tuesday "Substantial-Large/Extreme,"
Thursday Medium, Friday Substantial-Large; session focus unchanged (Monday/Thursday Aerobic
Capacity/UB with "Extensive Runs/Drills" replacing plain "Extensive Runs," Tuesday/Friday
Alactic Power/LB with "Sprints/Drills" replacing plain "Sprints").

The reference material behind this template sits on five image slides (p.5-10). p.5, "High
Intensity Training Components" (velocity-by-distance curve plus a table of exercise types by
distance band: Strength, Power, Power-Speed, Speed [Elastic Power], Special Endurance). p.6,
"High Intensity Training For Sports," reprints the same distance chart with sport-by-sport
high-intensity distance bars read off the chart: 200m Sprinter to about 200m, 100m Sprinter to
about 100m, Soccer Player to about 90m, Hockey Player to about 60m, "Football Player - Back"
to about 65m, Basketball Player to about 50m, "Football Player - Line" to about 35m, Thrower
to about 25m, Olympic Lifter to about 15m (note the chart says "Back," not "wide receiver," so
this is a position-group figure, not WR-specific). p.7, "Motor Unit Involvement," a bar chart
of approximate percentage of an athlete's total motor units by exercise, from 100% (Clean &
Jerk / Maximal Sprints) down to 5% (Seated Row / Isolated Supplementary Lifts). p.8,
"Training Zones of Physical Capacity," a five-zone table (purpose, magnitude, training method,
energetics, HR, lactate) credited "Borilkievich, V. Physical capacity in extreme muscle
conditions. Leningrad, USSR, 1982." p.9, a Jovanovic/Prilepin effort-level and reps/sets/volume
chart credited "Copyright 2013 by Mladen Jovanovic." p.10, an energy-system work:rest table
(type, intensity, duration, rest interval, number of sets, across alactic and glycolytic power
and capacity and aerobic power and capacity) with no sport or author label on the slide.

**Why it works** — Evans does not explain why this specific day-of-week loading pattern
(Tuesday and Friday as the two highest-load days, bracketing a Medium Monday and Thursday,
with three low/off days) was chosen over an alternative arrangement, nor why the General
sub-phase's 4-5 weeks shortens to 3-4 weeks in the Specific sub-phase; Inference: the
alactic-power/lower-body Tuesday-Friday pairing and aerobic-capacity/upper-body
Monday-Thursday pairing appears designed to separate the two energy-system emphases named in
the Step Five bioenergetic sequence (alactic and aerobic, see
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]) onto different training days
rather than combining them in the same session, consistent with the general
training-compatibility logic in [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]], but this
specific rationale is not stated by Evans in this lecture.

**When to apply** — As a concrete template for how a general-to-specific preparatory
progression can be laid out week-to-week for a skill-position football athlete, separating
aerobic-capacity/upper-body work from alactic-power/lower-body work by day. Eric's baseline
does not include a comparably detailed weekly loading template for any specific position.
`_book.md` records this course's Exam 3 Study Guide as cited once, for this entry, items 62
and 64-65 (see `_book.md` for the reconciliation); item 62 ("Alactic power speed distance
comparison between offensive lineman vs wide receiver") and items 64-65 (SPE/SDE lower-body
exercise choices for a wide receiver) confirm Evans intended a lineman-versus-wide-receiver
comparison as a further teaching point, but the specific comparative numbers for that
lineman/WR pairing were not found on the slide pages read for this ingest; the closest
figures actually on the slides are the p.6 "Back" versus "Line" position-group bars above, not
a lineman-versus-WR pairing.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an illustrative teaching template for a
hypothetical wide receiver, not data from any real athlete, team, or season; no actual
performance outcomes, injury data, or adherence data are given anywhere in this lecture to
support that this specific loading pattern is effective. The "8 hours per week (CARA)" and
NCAA-specific facility-availability framing tie this template to US college athletics
countable-hours rules, which Evans references elsewhere in the course as a real constraint
("NCAA reality? CARA hours..." U3 L3 p.12, p.16) but does not re-explain in this lecture; a
reader unfamiliar with NCAA countable-athletically-related-activity rules should not assume
this 8-hour figure applies outside that specific regulatory context. "CARA" itself is not
expanded on this slide; Inference (NCAA term): Countable Athletically Related Activities is
the entry writer's outside expansion of the acronym, not stated by Evans on this slide.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** — The weekly template itself, described above, plus the p.5-10 reference slides
(distance-by-intensity curve and sport bars, motor-unit-involvement chart, Borilkievich zones,
Jovanovic/Prilepin chart, energy-system work:rest table), is the example.

**Related** — [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]],
[[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]].

1	---
2	type: library-entry
3	kind: claim
4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
5	book: elite-sports-performance--evans
6	chapter: "U3 L1"
7	topic: sympathetic versus parasympathetic overtraining types, and an Omegawave HRV readiness case
8	category: [evans-citing, evans-framing, overtraining, monitoring, worked-example]
9	confidence: untested
10	ingest-tier: full-text
11	created: 2026-09-27
12	---
13	
14	# Overwork Splits Into Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Forms, Illustrated by an Omegawave HRV Case
15	
16	**What it is** — Evans's slides (U3 L1 p.15-18), following the four-stage Overtraining
17	Continuum (p.10, see [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]]) and the blunted
18	double-exercise-challenge finding (p.11: cortisol, ACTH, PRL, and GH response curves for OTS
19	[dashed] versus NFO [solid] athletes across two exercise challenges separated by rest, with
20	ACTH, PRL, and GH showing a markedly blunted second-challenge response in OTS, captioned "OTS
21	have blunted responses in double exercise challenges"), split "Overwork" into two forms.
22	Monotonous overwork: "Results in a plateau or decline in performance as a result of
23	over-adaptation of the CNS to the use of non-varying motor patterns." Overwork generally:
24	"Can occur when an increased training volume or intensity is sustained for too long or
25	repeated too frequently. This overwhelms the athlete's ability to adapt." This branches into
26	Sympathetic Overwork ("Prolonged stress response," p.16) and Parasympathetic Overwork
27	("Advanced stage of overtraining in which the neuroendocrine system is compromised," p.16). A
28	comparison table (p.17, "SNS vs PSNS Overwork") assigns Sympathetic overtraining to "Team
29	sports, strength and power sports" (decreased motivation, increased irritability and
30	depression; decreased appetite; increased resting/exercise/recovery heart rate and blood
31	pressure, increased ECG abnormalities; increased cortisol, decreased testosterone, decreased
32	testosterone/cortisol ratio, increased catecholamine concentration, increased postexercise
33	hormonal recovery time; decreased muscle and liver glycogen, variable lactate response;
34	chronic fatigue; decreased-or-unchanged performance), and Parasympathetic overtraining to
35	"Endurance sports" (increased listlessness, depression, and sleeping; unchanged appetite;
36	increased resting bradycardia, decreased-or-unchanged exercise heart rate, increased-or-
37	unchanged postexercise heart-rate recovery, decreased-or-unchanged blood-pressure response;
38	decreased responsiveness to stressors; increased hypoglycemia during exercise, decreased
39	exercise and postexercise lactate; increased fatigue; decreased-or-unchanged performance). A
40	second, separately numbered table (p.18, "Table-1: Distinguishing Symptoms of Sympathetic and
41	Parasympathetic overtraining [2]," the bracketed "[2]" indicating the slide reproduces a
42	citation from an outside source Evans does not name on the slide) gives a longer symptom list
43	by the same two categories: fatigue (both), irritability vs. calmness, sleeplessness vs.
44	normal sleep, lack of appetite vs. normal appetite, weight loss vs. no change in weight, easy
45	sweating vs. normal sweating, nocturnal sweating (sympathetic only), frequent headaches vs. no
46	headaches, palpitation/chest pain (sympathetic only), rapid resting pulse vs. normal pulse,
47	increased basal metabolism vs. normal, slightly increased body temperature vs. normal, delayed
48	vs. normal pulse-rate recovery, faster breathing rate during exercise vs. no breathing
49	problems, decreased tolerance to stress (sympathetic only), poor coordination vs. clumsy
50	movements and poor coordination especially during hard exercise, shortened vs. normal reaction
51	time, shaky hands (sympathetic only), and restlessness/depressed mood vs. normal mood.
52	
53	Immediately after (p.19-26), Evans presents six Omegawave HRV/readiness device screenshots for
54	what reads as a single unnamed athlete tracked over time (the screenshots are not individually
55	captioned with a name or date, so this continuity is Inference from the narrative sequence and
56	the p.24 "Comparing..." slide, not a stated fact). An early reading (p.19-20) shows: "Based on
57	the HRV assessment: Cardiac system is reasonably ready for any level of activity. Based on the
58	Omega assessment: CNS: High volume of Explosive and Explosive-Power activities are not
59	recommended." Readiness Indicators: Stress index 6 ("Within the norm"), Fatigue 7 ("Complete
60	recovery"), Adaptation reserves 6 ("High"); CNS 3 ("Reduced"); Metabolic reaction index 6,
61	value 400 (norm 100-500, "High"). The HRV detail slide (p.20) adds: "Stable adaptation to
62	stress. High functional reserve," bradycardia at 58 bpm, and parameters within norm (vagus
63	activity 0.28, norm 0.16-0.41; sympathetic activity 30, norm 15-55; tension index 54, norm
64	15-180). The spectrum breakdown (p.21) reads VLF 10.3%, LF 36.2%, HF 53.6%. A later reading
65	(p.22-23) shows decline: "Based on the HRV assessment: Active rest is preferred." Readiness
66	Indicators: Stress index 2 ("Distress"), Fatigue 1 ("Exhaustion"), Adaptation reserves 2
67	("Low"); Metabolic reaction index 5, value 269 ("Above average"). The HRV detail slide adds:
68	"Inadequate adaptation to stress. Low functional reserve. Excessive fatigue. Possible cardiac
69	system disturbance. Active rest preferred," tachycardia at 92 bpm, "Moderate sympathetic
70	hypertonia," and parameters outside norm (vagus activity 0.07, below the 0.16-0.41 norm;
71	tension index 582, far above the 15-180 norm). The p.24 "Comparing..." slide sets this reading
72	(VLF 16.6%, LF 43.0%, HF 40.4%) beside the earlier one. A further reading (p.25) is worse
73	still: "Unable to calculate spectrum due to significant rhythm disturbance." The final slide
74	(p.26) shows recovery, captioned "Blood work..." leading to "Less training / Improved
75	nutrition / Time," with the scattergram and histogram both tightening back toward the earlier,
76	healthier pattern.
77	
78	**Why it works** — Neither the overwork-type tables nor the Omegawave case gives a mechanism
79	beyond what is quoted; the tables state associations (which sport type tends toward which
80	overtraining form, which symptoms go with which form) without explaining the underlying
81	physiology, and the Omegawave case is a set of vendor-software readouts, not an explained
82	causal account of why the athlete's readiness declined. Inference: read together, the
83	sequence argues that HRV/readiness monitoring (Omegawave here) can track an athlete moving
84	along the sympathetic-overtraining pattern described on p.17 (elevated tension index and
85	sympathetic activity, reduced HRV) and back out of it, which is consistent with why this case
86	immediately follows the sympathetic/parasympathetic tables in the lecture's structure, though
87	Evans does not state that connection explicitly on these slides.
88	
89	**When to apply** — As a two-category vocabulary for describing which direction an
90	overtrained athlete's presentation points (sympathetic: irritable, tachycardic, high cortisol,
91	common in team/power sports; parasympathetic: listless, bradycardic, low responsiveness to
92	stressors, common in endurance sports), and as a worked illustration of what a declining and
93	recovering HRV/readiness trend can look like on one commercial device. Eric's baseline: it
94	does not name sympathetic/parasympathetic overtraining or use Omegawave specifically; its own
95	monitoring stack centers on force-plate mRSI and the VALD suite rather than HRV
96	(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring"). Inference: this framework
97	and case add HRV-specific vocabulary and a concrete device-output example not present in the
98	baseline material reviewed.
99	
100	**When NOT to apply** — The p.17 and p.18 tables carry no citation to a specific
101	paper on the slide itself (p.18's bracketed "[2]" shows the slide is reproducing someone
102	else's table, but the source is not named); do not treat the symptom lists as independently
103	verified without locating that source. The Omegawave case is a single unnamed athlete's
104	software output, not a validated case study with independent physiological confirmation, and
105	the entry writer's reading that all six screenshots belong to one athlete tracked over time is
106	Inference, not a stated fact on the slides. This entry also does not resolve, but records, a
107	tension elsewhere in the course: U3 L2 p.12 states the testosterone/cortisol ratio "used to be
108	considered the overtraining gold standard, but not anymore" (see
109	[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]), while this lecture's p.17
110	table lists a decreased testosterone/cortisol ratio as one of several sympathetic-overtraining
111	signs; both are recorded rather than reconciled. Confidence is untested.
112	
113	**Example** — The p.19-26 Omegawave readiness/HRV sequence, described in full above, is the
114	example: readiness index declining from "Complete recovery" (Fatigue 7, Stress index 6) to
115	"Distress / Exhaustion" (Fatigue 1, Stress index 2, tachycardia 92 bpm, tension index 582
116	against a 15-180 norm) to a reading where the spectrum could not be calculated "due to
117	significant rhythm disturbance," then recovering after "Blood work... Less training, Improved
118	nutrition, Time."
119	
120	**Related** — [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (the four-stage continuum
121	this material follows in the same lecture),
122	[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]] (U3 L2, the T/C-ratio
123	tension noted above, and Evans's later conclusion that HRV is "a great way to assess persons
124	ability to adapt to stressors" without being a stand-alone diagnostic).
125	</content>

common in team/power sports; parasympathetic: listless, bradycardic, low responsiveness to
stressors, common in endurance sports), and as a worked illustration of what a declining and
recovering HRV/readiness trend can look like on one commercial device. Eric's baseline: it
does not name sympathetic/parasympathetic overtraining or use Omegawave specifically; its own
monitoring stack centers on force-plate mRSI and the VALD suite rather than HRV
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring"). Inference: this framework
and case add HRV-specific vocabulary and a concrete device-output example not present in the
baseline material reviewed.

**When NOT to apply** — The p.17 and p.18 tables carry no citation to a specific
paper on the slide itself (p.18's bracketed "[2]" shows the slide is reproducing someone
else's table, but the source is not named); do not treat the symptom lists as independently
verified without locating that source. The Omegawave case is a single unnamed athlete's
software output, not a validated case study with independent physiological confirmation, and
the entry writer's reading that all six screenshots belong to one athlete tracked over time is
Inference, not a stated fact on the slides. This entry also does not resolve, but records, a
tension elsewhere in the course: U3 L2 p.12 states the testosterone/cortisol ratio "used to be
considered the overtraining gold standard, but not anymore" (see
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]), while this lecture's p.17
table lists a decreased testosterone/cortisol ratio as one of several sympathetic-overtraining
signs; both are recorded rather than reconciled. Confidence is untested.

**Example** — The p.19-26 Omegawave readiness/HRV sequence, described in full above, is the
example: readiness index declining from "Complete recovery" (Fatigue 7, Stress index 6) to
"Distress / Exhaustion" (Fatigue 1, Stress index 2, tachycardia 92 bpm, tension index 582
against a 15-180 norm) to a reading where the spectrum could not be calculated "due to
significant rhythm disturbance," then recovering after "Blood work... Less training, Improved
nutrition, Time."

**Related** — [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (the four-stage continuum
this material follows in the same lecture),
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]] (U3 L2, the T/C-ratio
tension noted above, and Evans's later conclusion that HRV is "a great way to assess persons
ability to adapt to stressors" without being a stand-alone diagnostic).
</content>

domain: strength-and-conditioning

topic: sympathetic versus parasympathetic overtraining types, and an Omegawave HRV readiness case
category: [evans-citing, evans-framing, overtraining, monitoring, worked-example]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27

# Overwork Splits Into Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Forms, Illustrated by an Omegawave HRV Case

**What it is** — Evans's slides (U3 L1 p.15-18), following the four-stage Overtraining
Continuum (p.10, see [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]]) and the blunted
double-exercise-challenge finding (p.11: cortisol, ACTH, PRL, and GH response curves for OTS
[dashed] versus NFO [solid] athletes across two exercise challenges separated by rest, with
ACTH, PRL, and GH showing a markedly blunted second-challenge response in OTS, captioned "OTS
have blunted responses in double exercise challenges"), split overtraining into types. The
slides split "Overtraining" into Monotonous ("Results in a plateau or decline in performance
as a result of over-adaptation of the CNS to the use of non-varying motor patterns") and
Overwork ("Can occur when an increased training volume or intensity is sustained for too long
or repeated too frequently. This overwhelms the athlete's ability to adapt") (p.15). Only
Overwork splits further, into Sympathetic Overwork and Parasympathetic Overwork (p.15-16). The
p.16 slide, titled "SNS vs PSNS Overwork," defines SNS as "Prolonged stress response" and PSNS
as "Advanced stage of overtraining in which the neuroendocrine system is compromised."

A comparison table (p.17, untitled; the p.16 title is "SNS vs PSNS Overwork") assigns
Sympathetic to "Team sports, strength and power sports" (decreased motivation, increased
irritability and depression; decreased appetite; increased resting/exercise/recovery heart
rate and blood pressure, increased ECG abnormalities; increased cortisol, decreased
testosterone, decreased testosterone/cortisol ratio, increased catecholamine concentration,
increased postexercise hormonal recovery time; decreased muscle and liver glycogen, variable
lactate response; chronic fatigue; decreased-or-unchanged performance), and Parasympathetic to
"Endurance sports" (increased listlessness, depression, and sleeping; unchanged appetite;
increased resting bradycardia, decreased-or-unchanged exercise heart rate, increased-or-
unchanged postexercise heart-rate recovery, decreased-or-unchanged blood-pressure response;
decreased responsiveness to stressors; increased hypoglycemia during exercise, decreased
exercise and postexercise lactate; increased fatigue; decreased-or-unchanged performance). A
second table (p.18, "Table-1: Distinguishing Symptoms of Sympathetic and Parasympathetic
overtraining [2]") gives a longer symptom list by the same two categories: fatigue (both),
irritability vs. calmness, sleeplessness vs. normal sleep, lack of appetite vs. normal
appetite, weight loss vs. no change in weight, easy sweating vs. normal sweating, nocturnal
sweating (sympathetic only), frequent headaches vs. no headaches, palpitation, heaviness and
stabbing pain in chest (sympathetic only), rapid resting pulse vs. normal pulse, increased
basal metabolism vs. normal, slightly increased body temperature vs. normal, delayed vs.
normal pulse-rate recovery, faster breathing rate during exercise vs. no breathing problems,
decreased tolerance to stress (sympathetic only), poor coordination vs. "Climsy [sic]
movements and poor coordination specially during hard exercise," shortened vs. normal reaction
time, shaky hands (sympathetic only), and restlessness/depressed mood vs. normal mood. The
slides reproduce both tables with no attribution shown beyond the bracketed "[2]" on p.18.
Inference: the bracketed "[2]" suggests a table reproduced from a numbered source the slide
does not name.

Immediately after (p.19-26), eight slides hold ten Omegawave HRV/readiness screenshots (p.24
and p.26 each hold two panels). The screenshots are not captioned with a name or date, so
reading them as one unnamed athlete tracked over time is Inference from the sequence and the
p.24 "Comparing..." slide. An early reading (p.19) shows: "Based on the HRV assessment:
Cardiac system is reasonably ready for any level of activity. Based on the Omega assessment:
CNS: High volume of Explosive and Explosive-Power activities are not recommended." Readiness
Indicators: Stress index 6 ("Within the norm"), Fatigue 7 ("Complete recovery"), Adaptation
reserves 6 ("High"); CNS 3 ("Reduced"); Metabolic reaction index grade 6, value 400 (norm
100-500, "High"). The HRV detail slide (p.20) adds: "Stable adaptation to stress. High
functional reserve," bradycardia at 58 bpm, parameters within norm (vagus activity 0.28, norm
0.16-0.41; sympathetic activity 30, norm 15-55; tension index 54, norm 15-180) and RMSSD 68.
The spectrum breakdown (p.21) reads VLF 10.3%, LF 36.2%, HF 53.6%. A later reading (p.22)
shows decline: "Based on the HRV assessment: Active rest is preferred." Readiness Indicators:
Stress index 2 ("Distress"), Fatigue 1 ("Exhaustion"), Adaptation reserves 2 ("Low");
Metabolic reaction index grade 5, value 269 ("Above average"). Its HRV detail slide (p.23)
adds: "Inadequate adaptation to stress. Low functional reserve. Excessive fatigue. Possible
cardiac system disturbance. Active rest preferred," tachycardia at 92 bpm, "Moderate
sympathetic hypertonia," and RMSSD 7. Four p.23 values are marked red, outside norm: vagus
activity 0.07 (norm 0.16-0.41), tension index 582 (norm 15-180), "Share of the aperiodic
influences" 3.96 (norm 1.25-3.05), and "Standard deviation of the aspirate waves" 0.004 (norm
0.018-0.054). Sympathetic activity is 53, within its 15-55 norm. The p.24 "Comparing..."
slide sets the earlier spectrum (left) beside a later one (right: VLF 16.6%, LF 43.0%, HF
40.4%). The pairs reconcile numerically: p.20 HF n.u. 59.7 = 53.6 / (53.6 + 36.2) from p.21,
and p.23 LF n.u. 51.6 = 43.0 / (43.0 + 40.4) from the p.24 right panel, which supports reading
p.20-21 as one recording and p.22-24 (right) as another. A further reading (p.25, order not
stated) shows a rhythm disturbance at a lower heart rate: "Unable to calculate spectrum due to
significant rhythm disturbance." The final slide (p.26) shows two panels captioned "Blood
work..." and "Less training / Improved nutrition / Time," with the scattergram and histogram
tightening in the second panel.

p.27, still inside this section, lists overtraining-syndrome signs under five headings
(Physiological, Immunological, Biochemical, Performance, Psychological), with a "[86]"
reference marker; its Biochemical list includes "Increased serum cortisol and SHBG,"
"Decreased serum testosterone," and "Decreased testosterone : cortisol."

**Why it works** — Neither the overwork-type tables nor the Omegawave case gives a mechanism
beyond what is quoted; the tables state associations (which sport type tends toward which
overtraining form, which symptoms go with which form) without explaining the underlying
physiology, and the Omegawave case is a set of vendor-software readouts, not an explained
causal account of why the athlete's readiness declined. Inference: read together, the
sequence argues that HRV/readiness monitoring (Omegawave here) can track an athlete moving
toward the sympathetic pattern on p.17 and back out of it: elevated tension index, reduced
vagal activity and HRV (RMSSD 68 -> 7); sympathetic activity rose (30 -> 53) but stayed within
norm. The slides do not state that connection.

**When to apply** — As a two-category vocabulary for describing which direction an
overworked athlete's presentation points (sympathetic: irritable, tachycardic, high cortisol,
common in team/power sports; parasympathetic: listless, bradycardic, low responsiveness to
stressors, common in endurance sports), and as a worked illustration of what a declining and
recovering HRV/readiness trend can look like on one commercial device. Eric's baseline: it
does not mention HRV or Omegawave; its daily readiness marker is force-plate mRSI
(`method-baseline.md` line 58), and the stack lists Polar heart rate (line 155). Inference:
this entry adds HRV-specific vocabulary and a concrete device-output example not present in
the baseline material reviewed.

**When NOT to apply** — The p.17, p.18 and p.27 tables carry no named source on the slides
(only the bracketed "[2]" on p.18 and "[86]" on p.27); do not treat the symptom lists as
independently verified without locating those sources. Not verified here: the p.17 layout
may resemble Kreher and Schwartz (2012, *Sports Health*), "Overtraining syndrome: a practical
guide." The Omegawave case is unnamed software output, not a validated case study with
independent physiological confirmation, and reading all ten screenshots as one athlete
tracked over time is Inference. The slides give no dates, so the order of p.25 relative to
p.22-24 is not stated. This entry also records, without resolving, a tension elsewhere in the
course: U3 L2 p.12 states the testosterone/cortisol ratio "used to be considered the
overtraining gold standard, but not anymore" (see
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]), while this lecture lists
a decreased testosterone/cortisol ratio as a sympathetic-overtraining sign (p.17) and as an
OTS biochemical sign (p.27); both are recorded rather than reconciled. Confidence is untested.

**Example** — The p.19-26 Omegawave readiness/HRV sequence, described above, is the example:
readiness indicators moving from "Complete recovery" (Fatigue 7, Stress index 6) to "Distress
/ Exhaustion" (Fatigue 1, Stress index 2, tachycardia 92 bpm, tension index 582 against a
15-180 norm), a reading (order not stated) where the spectrum could not be calculated "due to
significant rhythm disturbance," and a final slide captioned "Blood work..." and "Less
training / Improved nutrition / Time."

**Related** — [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (the four-stage continuum
this material follows in the same lecture),
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]] (U3 L2, the T/C-ratio
tension noted above, and Evans's later conclusion that HRV is "a great way to assess persons
ability to adapt to stressors" without being a stand-alone diagnostic).

# Overwork Splits Into Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Forms, Illustrated by an Omegawave HRV Case

**What it is** — Evans's slides (U3 L1 p.15-18), following the four-stage Overtraining
Continuum (p.10, see [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]]) and the blunted
double-exercise-challenge finding (p.11: cortisol, ACTH, PRL, and GH response curves for OTS
[dashed] versus NFO [solid] athletes across two exercise challenges separated by rest, with
ACTH, PRL, and GH showing a markedly blunted second-challenge response in OTS, captioned "OTS
have blunted responses in double exercise challenges"), split "Overwork" into two forms.
Monotonous overwork: "Results in a plateau or decline in performance as a result of
over-adaptation of the CNS to the use of non-varying motor patterns." Overwork generally:
"Can occur when an increased training volume or intensity is sustained for too long or
repeated too frequently. This overwhelms the athlete's ability to adapt." This branches into
Sympathetic Overwork ("Prolonged stress response," p.16) and Parasympathetic Overwork
("Advanced stage of overtraining in which the neuroendocrine system is compromised," p.16). A
comparison table (p.17, "SNS vs PSNS Overwork") assigns Sympathetic overtraining to "Team
sports, strength and power sports" (decreased motivation, increased irritability and
depression; decreased appetite; increased resting/exercise/recovery heart rate and blood
pressure, increased ECG abnormalities; increased cortisol, decreased testosterone, decreased
testosterone/cortisol ratio, increased catecholamine concentration, increased postexercise
hormonal recovery time; decreased muscle and liver glycogen, variable lactate response;
chronic fatigue; decreased-or-unchanged performance), and Parasympathetic overtraining to
"Endurance sports" (increased listlessness, depression, and sleeping; unchanged appetite;
increased resting bradycardia, decreased-or-unchanged exercise heart rate, increased-or-
unchanged postexercise heart-rate recovery, decreased-or-unchanged blood-pressure response;
decreased responsiveness to stressors; increased hypoglycemia during exercise, decreased
exercise and postexercise lactate; increased fatigue; decreased-or-unchanged performance). A
second, separately numbered table (p.18, "Table-1: Distinguishing Symptoms of Sympathetic and
Parasympathetic overtraining [2]," the bracketed "[2]" indicating the slide reproduces a
citation from an outside source Evans does not name on the slide) gives a longer symptom list
by the same two categories: fatigue (both), irritability vs. calmness, sleeplessness vs.
normal sleep, lack of appetite vs. normal appetite, weight loss vs. no change in weight, easy
sweating vs. normal sweating, nocturnal sweating (sympathetic only), frequent headaches vs. no
headaches, palpitation/chest pain (sympathetic only), rapid resting pulse vs. normal pulse,
increased basal metabolism vs. normal, slightly increased body temperature vs. normal, delayed
vs. normal pulse-rate recovery, faster breathing rate during exercise vs. no breathing
problems, decreased tolerance to stress (sympathetic only), poor coordination vs. clumsy
movements and poor coordination especially during hard exercise, shortened vs. normal reaction
time, shaky hands (sympathetic only), and restlessness/depressed mood vs. normal mood.

Immediately after (p.19-26), Evans presents six Omegawave HRV/readiness device screenshots for
what reads as a single unnamed athlete tracked over time (the screenshots are not individually
captioned with a name or date, so this continuity is Inference from the narrative sequence and
the p.24 "Comparing..." slide, not a stated fact). An early reading (p.19-20) shows: "Based on
the HRV assessment: Cardiac system is reasonably ready for any level of activity. Based on the
Omega assessment: CNS: High volume of Explosive and Explosive-Power activities are not
recommended." Readiness Indicators: Stress index 6 ("Within the norm"), Fatigue 7 ("Complete
recovery"), Adaptation reserves 6 ("High"); CNS 3 ("Reduced"); Metabolic reaction index 6,
value 400 (norm 100-500, "High"). The HRV detail slide (p.20) adds: "Stable adaptation to
stress. High functional reserve," bradycardia at 58 bpm, and parameters within norm (vagus
activity 0.28, norm 0.16-0.41; sympathetic activity 30, norm 15-55; tension index 54, norm
15-180). The spectrum breakdown (p.21) reads VLF 10.3%, LF 36.2%, HF 53.6%. A later reading
(p.22-23) shows decline: "Based on the HRV assessment: Active rest is preferred." Readiness
Indicators: Stress index 2 ("Distress"), Fatigue 1 ("Exhaustion"), Adaptation reserves 2
("Low"); Metabolic reaction index 5, value 269 ("Above average"). The HRV detail slide adds:
"Inadequate adaptation to stress. Low functional reserve. Excessive fatigue. Possible cardiac
system disturbance. Active rest preferred," tachycardia at 92 bpm, "Moderate sympathetic
hypertonia," and parameters outside norm (vagus activity 0.07, below the 0.16-0.41 norm;
tension index 582, far above the 15-180 norm). The p.24 "Comparing..." slide sets this reading
(VLF 16.6%, LF 43.0%, HF 40.4%) beside the earlier one. A further reading (p.25) is worse
still: "Unable to calculate spectrum due to significant rhythm disturbance." The final slide
(p.26) shows recovery, captioned "Blood work..." leading to "Less training / Improved
nutrition / Time," with the scattergram and histogram both tightening back toward the earlier,
healthier pattern.

**Why it works** — Neither the overwork-type tables nor the Omegawave case gives a mechanism
beyond what is quoted; the tables state associations (which sport type tends toward which
overtraining form, which symptoms go with which form) without explaining the underlying
physiology, and the Omegawave case is a set of vendor-software readouts, not an explained
causal account of why the athlete's readiness declined. Inference: read together, the
sequence argues that HRV/readiness monitoring (Omegawave here) can track an athlete moving
along the sympathetic-overtraining pattern described on p.17 (elevated tension index and
sympathetic activity, reduced HRV) and back out of it, which is consistent with why this case
immediately follows the sympathetic/parasympathetic tables in the lecture's structure, though
Evans does not state that connection explicitly on these slides.

**When to apply** — As a two-category vocabulary for describing which direction an
overtrained athlete's presentation points (sympathetic: irritable, tachycardic, high cortisol,
common in team/power sports; parasympathetic: listless, bradycardic, low responsiveness to
stressors, common in endurance sports), and as a worked illustration of what a declining and
recovering HRV/readiness trend can look like on one commercial device. Eric's baseline: it
does not name sympathetic/parasympathetic overtraining or use Omegawave specifically; its own
monitoring stack centers on force-plate mRSI and the VALD suite rather than HRV
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring"). Inference: this framework
and case add HRV-specific vocabulary and a concrete device-output example not present in the
baseline material reviewed.

**When NOT to apply** — The p.17 and p.18 tables carry no citation to a specific
paper on the slide itself (p.18's bracketed "[2]" shows the slide is reproducing someone
else's table, but the source is not named); do not treat the symptom lists as independently
verified without locating that source. The Omegawave case is a single unnamed athlete's
software output, not a validated case study with independent physiological confirmation, and
the entry writer's reading that all six screenshots belong to one athlete tracked over time is
Inference, not a stated fact on the slides. This entry also does not resolve, but records, a
tension elsewhere in the course: U3 L2 p.12 states the testosterone/cortisol ratio "used to be
considered the overtraining gold standard, but not anymore" (see
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]), while this lecture's p.17
table lists a decreased testosterone/cortisol ratio as one of several sympathetic-overtraining
signs; both are recorded rather than reconciled. Confidence is untested.

**Example** — The p.19-26 Omegawave readiness/HRV sequence, described in full above, is the
example: readiness index declining from "Complete recovery" (Fatigue 7, Stress index 6) to
"Distress / Exhaustion" (Fatigue 1, Stress index 2, tachycardia 92 bpm, tension index 582
against a 15-180 norm) to a reading where the spectrum could not be calculated "due to
significant rhythm disturbance," then recovering after "Blood work... Less training, Improved
nutrition, Time."

**Related** — [[framework--overtraining-continuum-for-nfor-ots]] (the four-stage continuum
this material follows in the same lecture),
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]] (U3 L2, the T/C-ratio
tension noted above, and Evans's later conclusion that HRV is "a great way to assess persons
ability to adapt to stressors" without being a stand-alone diagnostic).
</content>

**Why it works** — Evans's own stated reasoning is that weight-room exercises typically meet
only some of the Dynamic Correspondence criteria (see
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]] for the five-factor
checklist) relative to a given sport's actual competitive movements, so a weight-room test
result (e.g., a back squat max) does not directly indicate how that capacity will express
itself in the sport-specific movement pattern; he does not, in this slide, specify which of the
five Dynamic Correspondence criteria weight-room exercises typically fail, only that "minimal
DC criteria" are met in general.

====L

`supertraining--verkhoshansky/_book.md` and `transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/_book.md`
could each note that this course-lecture entry independently lists their authors among a
lineage of "giants," as a light corroboration of those authors' standing in the field
(not of any specific claim).
</content>
====O

**When to apply** — As a three-way classification for describing the intent of a given
training block or phase: is this phase meant to stimulate new adaptation, retain current
fitness during a competing priority (e.g., in-season), or is it a planned detraining/deload
period. Eric's baseline: its in-season rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`). Inference: this functions as a
===G
# Bill Sands's "Performance Garden": Training Plans [sic] Seeds, Rest Lets Them Grow, Judgment Lets Them Bear Fruit

**What it is** — Evans's slide (U3 L4 p.21) credits "Bill Sands, Performance Garden" with a
three-part metaphor: "Training - Plan seeds. Rest/Recovery - Allow plants to grow. With
Intelligence & Common Sense - Allow Plants to Bear Fruit." (The slide reads "Training - Plan
seeds"; "Plan" is probably a typo for "Plant" given the surrounding garden imagery, but the
slide is not corrected here since the intended word cannot be confirmed.) No further citation
(publication, year, or context) is given for this metaphor beyond the named source.

**Why it works** — This is an explicitly metaphorical framing, not a mechanism claim; the
slide gives no biological or training-science content beyond the analogy itself. Inference:
the three-part structure maps training to input (planting), recovery to a necessary
maturation period the coach cannot rush (growth), and coaching judgment to the factor that
converts potential into realized result (fruit) - paralleling the course's broader theme
(seen also in [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]] and
[[principle--recovery-is-a-training-means]]) that recovery is an active, necessary phase, not
a passive gap, and that judgment/timing matters as much as the training stimulus itself.

**When to apply** — As a communication device when explaining to athletes or staff why a
taper or rest period is a planned part of the process rather than "doing nothing." No
directly equivalent metaphor appears in Eric's baseline, though Eric's baseline states that
"recovery has to be earned by training hard first" and that recovery technology "is useful
but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Recovery and sleep"). Inference: this shares the underlying premise that training and
recovery are sequential, interdependent phases rather than substitutes for each other.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication metaphor, not a testable claim;
it should not be cited as evidence for any specific training or recovery prescription.
Confidence is untested, and the entry writer has not located or verified an original Bill
Sands publication or presentation this metaphor is drawn from within this ingest.

**Example** — The metaphor itself, as quoted above, is the only content given.

**Related** — [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]],
[[principle--recovery-is-a-training-means]].

content.content:
**What it is** — Evans's slides (U1 L4 p.17-22) present two distinct regulatory models. He
credits "1935 - Walter Cannon" with Homeostasis: "Processes in the organism to preserve
constant conditions within which are centered around specific set points and governed by
negative feedback loops" (p.15). He credits "Sterling & Sayer in 1988" (the slide's spelling;
the well-known 1988 paper is by Sterling and Eyer; Inference (reviewer knowledge): this is the
entry writer's outside identification, not stated on the slide) and "Jay Schulkin" with
Allostasis: "Process by which an organism achieves internal viability through a bodily change
of state," further distinguishing "Allostatic State" ("Chronic OVER-ACTIVATION of regulatory
systems and the alterations of body set points") from "Allostatic Overload" ("expression of
pathophysiology by the chronic over-activation of regulating systems") (p.17). A
direct-comparison slide (p.19), which carries no attribution on the slide itself, states:
"Homeostasis describes mechanisms that HOLD CONSTANT a controlled variable by sensing its
deviation from a 'setpoint' and feeding back to correct the error. Allostasis describes
mechanisms that CHANGE a controlled variable by predicting what level will be needed and
overriding local feedback to meet anticipated demand." The following slide (p.20), credited to
"Bruce McEwen," adds a qualifier the p.19 comparison slide does not carry: "Some systems
operate under the homeostasis model: Thermal Regulation, Oxygen Tension, pH Levels." The
worked example given is blood pressure: "120/80 is 'normal.' What happens if it jumps up to
150/100?" with the answer, credited to "(Sterling, Eyer, 1998)" on the following slide (note:
this citation year, 1998, differs from the 1988 year given two slides earlier for the same
Sterling and Eyer source; the slide deck does not reconcile this discrepancy, so both years
are recorded here as they appear): "Brain sets blood pressure via multiple, mutually
reinforcing mechanisms. Negative feedback mechanisms are acutely overridden. When demand
persists, all mechanisms are reset to operate at the new level."

**Why it works** — The slides state the distinction (fixed setpoint with feedback correction,
versus a setpoint that shifts to anticipate demand) but do not explain the underlying neural
or endocrine mechanism connecting a training stimulus to a shifted setpoint beyond the blood
pressure example; the p.22 diagram names the mechanisms (cardiac output, vasoconstriction,
renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone, cortisol, ACTH, CRH, vasopressin, ANP, norepinephrine, the
autonomic nervous system, and Na/H2O retention) but does not explain how any one of them
works. Inference: applied to training adaptation, the distinction implies that some
training-induced changes (e.g., a durably raised resting heart rate range under chronic
overreaching) may be better modeled as an allostatic setpoint shift than as homeostatic
disturbance-and-recovery, but Evans does not make this application explicit in this lecture;
it is a plausible follow-on question left open by his own subsequent slides on
Verkhoshansky's training-load-to-allostatic-overload model (U1 L4 p.26-33), atomized
separately in this ingest, see
[[framework--verkhoshansky-activation-levels-and-threshold-of-adaptability]].

**When to apply** — As a vocabulary distinction when discussing whether an athlete's altered
baseline (elevated resting HR, altered HRV baseline, elevated resting blood pressure) under
sustained hard training reflects a genuine allostatic setpoint shift versus ordinary
homeostatic strain that will resolve with recovery. Eric's baseline: it discusses
HRV-adjacent and readiness-monitoring concepts without using homeostasis/allostasis
vocabulary specifically (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"
"Recovery and sleep"). Inference: this framework offers language not currently present in the
baseline, though its practical application to Baylor's monitoring stack is not demonstrated
by Evans in this lecture.

**When NOT to apply** — The citation years for Sterling and Eyer are internally
inconsistent on Evans's own slides (1988 on p.17, 1998 on p.22); this entry records both as
written rather than silently picking one. The p.19 direct-comparison slide itself carries no
attribution; only the p.20 qualifier slide names McEwen. The blood pressure example is
illustrative, not a worked case with real data; no actual athlete or training example is
given anywhere in this segment of the lecture. Confidence is untested.

**Example** — The blood pressure "120/80 to 150/100" illustration described above is the
lecture's only worked example, and it is hypothetical, not a real measured case.

**Related** — [[framework--verkhoshansky-activation-levels-and-threshold-of-adaptability]]
(Evans's own next slides, U1 L4 p.26-33, applying the allostasis/allostatic-overload
vocabulary directly to training load). Reciprocal-link suggestion:
`supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation.md` and
`supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus.md` cover
Verkhoshansky's training-load-to-adaptation model; a reviewer with both books staged should
check whether Evans's 2012-cited version adds or conflicts with anything in those two
Supertraining entries. Vault link: `research-papers/mcewen-2000-allostasis-and-allostatic
-load-implications-for-neuropsychopharmacology.md`, if staged, should be checked for whether
it corroborates the p.19-20 comparison and qualifier.
</content>

Sterling and Eyer source; the slide deck does not reconcile this discrepancy, so both years
are recorded here as they appear): "Brain sets blood pressure via multiple, mutually
reinforcing mechanisms. Negative feedback mechanisms are acutely overridden. When demand
persists, all mechanisms are reset to operate at the new level."

**Why it works** — The slides state the distinction (fixed setpoint with feedback correction,
versus a setpoint that shifts to anticipate demand) but do not explain the underlying neural
or endocrine mechanism connecting a training stimulus to a shifted setpoint beyond the blood
pressure example; the p.22 diagram names the mechanisms (cardiac output, vasoconstriction,
renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone, cortisol, ACTH, CRH, vasopressin, ANP, norepinephrine, the
autonomic nervous system, and Na/H2O retention) but does not explain how any one of them
works. Inference: applied to training adaptation, the distinction implies that some
training-induced changes (e.g., a durably raised resting heart rate range under chronic
overreaching) may be better modeled as an allostatic setpoint shift than as homeostatic
disturbance-and-recovery, but Evans does not make this application explicit in this lecture;
it is a plausible follow-on question left open by his own subsequent slides on
Verkhoshansky's training-load-to-allostatic-overload model (U1 L4 p.26-33), atomized
separately in this ingest, see
[[framework--verkhoshansky-activation-levels-and-threshold-of-adaptability]].

**When to apply** — As a vocabulary distinction when discussing whether an athlete's altered
baseline (elevated resting HR, altered HRV baseline, elevated resting blood pressure) under
sustained hard training reflects a genuine allostatic setpoint shift versus ordinary
homeostatic strain that will resolve with recovery. Eric's baseline: it discusses
HRV-adjacent and readiness-monitoring concepts without using homeostasis/allostasis
vocabulary specifically (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring,"

baseline, though its practical application to Baylor's monitoring stack is not demonstrated
by Evans in this lecture.

inconsistent on Evans's own slides (1988 on p.17, 1998 on p.22); this entry records both as

attribution; only the p.20 qualifier slide names McEwen. The blood pressure example is
illustrative, not a worked case with real data; no actual athlete or training example is

# Evans's Framing of the Periodization Evidence Debate: "Classic" Versus "Non-Classic" Literature

**What it is** — Evans's slides (U3 L4 p.13-14), titled "Literature Issue," present two
opposing characterizations of the periodization research base, the slides state (no attribution shown).
Non-classic literature (his term for research not from Eastern Europe or the Soviet Union) is
described as: "Suggestive there is little research to support Periodization. Very few elite
athletes are used in the research. Short term studies. One dimensional. Non-classic believes
phrasing as its sparse text allows). The following slides (p.7-9) list body-composition models
(Two, Three, and Four Compartment) and the most widely used field methods (Hydrostatic
Weighing, BodPod, DEXA, Bioelectrical Impedance, Skinfolds). The p.9 error-rate slide is laid
out in three blocks: "Small Error Rates for Populations" - Underwater Weighing (UW) 0.1-2.1%,
BodPod (BP) 2%, Skinfolds (SF) 6%, DEXA 1-2%, alongside a separate list of population-level
error sources ("Ethnicity, Age, Gender..."); "Large Error Rates for Individuals" - UW 5%+, BP
6%+, Bioelectrical Impedance (BIA) 8-9% (BIA has no population-level figure; 8-9% is its only
figure on this slide), Skinfolds 10-15%, DEXA 4-10%; and, set apart under its own heading,
"Tracking over time... different? SF: 3-5%."

**Why it works** — Evans's own reasoning is that only carcass analysis (necessarily
post-mortem) directly measures body fat, so every practical field method is instead a
statistical prediction from indirect proxies; this is a stated epistemic point about
measurement validity, not a physiological mechanism claim. Inference: the practical
implication is that population-level error rates (the more favorable numbers in the table)
should not be mistaken for individual-athlete accuracy, since the same slide explicitly
separates population from individual error and reports individual-level error as higher for
every method that has both figures (BIA has only the individual-level figure, so no
within-method comparison is possible for it).

**When to apply** — As a caution when reporting or discussing body-composition numbers with
Training Load, "Best athletes," ES, $), Strain (Monotony x Weekly Training Load, "Best
athletes," ES, $), Heart Rate Variability ("√ or Best Athletes," ED, $-$$$). ("ES" and "ED"
are used on the slide without a stated legend; Inference: likely "Every Session" and "Every
Day" respectively, given the monitoring-schedule table on the following page (p.22) uses "ED"
for HRV and "ES" for RPE and Bosco jump testing, both of which are typically administered
daily or every session.)

**Why it works** — The slides state which tools exist and at what frequency and (for
Psychological and Physical Fitness) cost, but do not explain why each specific frequency was
p.16 "Body Comp Analyzers... no more than 4x per year" figure matches, number for number, the

composition," line 130, citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`); this slide may be the
origin of, or a shared source with, that baseline rule, though this is not confirmed.

slide itself; the reading given above is Inference from context (the monitoring-schedule table

body fat measured?" (paraphrased rhetorical framing, quoted as close to the slide's own

illustration; no specific athlete case is given.

method error rates at population versus individual level (checked by grep for "DEXA" and
"body composition" combined with "error rate").
